title: What is the JDK Flow API introduced in Java 9? Explain Publisher, Subscriber, Subscription and Processor, how they implement the Reactive Streams specification, and how `Subscription.request(n)` provides demand-based backpressure.
shortTitle: What is the JDK Flow API?

s1_definition.profdef: The Flow API is a small set of four nested interfaces inside `java.util.concurrent.Flow` — `Publisher`, `Subscriber`, `Subscription` and `Processor` — added in Java 9. They are the JDK's standard adoption of the Reactive Streams specification, which defines a protocol for asynchronous stream processing with non-blocking backpressure. Backpressure means the consumer tells the producer exactly how many items it is ready to receive by calling `Subscription.request(n)`, so a fast producer can never overwhelm a slow consumer.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh is a fast teller at National Bank of India who can stamp a thousand cheques a minute, and Priya is an auditor who can only verify ten cheques a minute. If Rajesh just keeps throwing stamped cheques at Priya, her desk overflows and cheques fall on the floor (memory overflow). Instead, Priya shouts "send me ten" and Rajesh sends exactly ten. When she finishes, she shouts "send me ten more". That shouting is `request(n)`. Priya controls the pace, not Rajesh. This is backpressure — the consumer pulls as much as it can handle while the producer pushes within that limit.
s1_definition.oneliner: Flow API is the JDK's four-interface Reactive Streams contract where the subscriber calls `request(n)` to pull demand so a fast publisher never floods a slow consumer.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Flow API is a small set of four nested interfaces inside `java.util.concurrent.Flow` — `Publisher`, `Subscriber`, `Subscription` and `Processor` — added in Java 9. They are the JDK's standard adoption of the Reactive Streams specification, which defines a protocol for asynchronous stream processing with non-blocking backpressure. Backpressure means the consumer tells the producer exactly how many items it is ready to receive by calling `Subscription.request(n)`, so a fast producer can never overwhelm a slow consumer.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh is a fast teller at National Bank of India who can stamp a thousand cheques a minute, and Priya is an auditor who can only verify ten cheques a minute. If Rajesh just keeps throwing stamped cheques at Priya, her desk overflows and cheques fall on the floor (memory overflow). Instead, Priya shouts "send me ten" and Rajesh sends exactly ten. When she finishes, she shouts "send me ten more". That shouting is `request(n)`. Priya controls the pace, not Rajesh. This is backpressure — the consumer pulls as much as it can handle while the producer pushes within that limit.

**One line to remember:** Flow API is the JDK's four-interface Reactive Streams contract where the subscriber calls `request(n)` to pull demand so a fast publisher never floods a slow consumer.

sections.s2_technical:
The `Flow` class is just a container; the real contract is in its four nested interfaces. A `Flow.Publisher<T>` is a source of items and has a single method `subscribe(Subscriber<? super T> s)`. When you subscribe, the publisher must hand back a `Subscription` by calling the subscriber's `onSubscribe` method. For example, a transaction feed publisher is declared as `class TxnPublisher implements Flow.Publisher<Transaction>` and its `subscribe` method creates a subscription object and calls `subscriber.onSubscribe(subscription)`.

A `Flow.Subscriber<T>` is the consumer. It has four callbacks. `onSubscribe(Subscription s)` receives the subscription and is where the subscriber decides its initial demand, for example `s.request(10)` to ask for ten transactions. `onNext(T item)` delivers one item at a time, for example `onNext(transaction)` where the subscriber verifies the transaction and then calls `subscription.request(1)` to ask for the next one. `onError(Throwable t)` is called once if the stream fails, for example a database connection drop, and no further items arrive. `onComplete()` is called once when the stream ends normally with no more items.

A `Flow.Subscription` is the private channel between one publisher and one subscriber. It has two methods. `request(long n)` tells the publisher the subscriber is ready for `n` more items; this is the heart of backpressure. For example `subscription.request(5)` means "I can handle five more settlements now". `cancel()` tells the publisher to stop sending, for example when the auditor closes the session: `subscription.cancel()`.

A `Flow.Processor<T,R>` is both a subscriber and a publisher at the same time; it consumes items of type T and republishes transformed items of type R. For example a `FeeEnrichmentProcessor implements Flow.Processor<Transaction, EnrichedTransaction>` subscribes upstream to raw transactions, adds a calculated fee, and publishes enriched transactions downstream. Processors let you build pipelines like raw feed, then fee enrichment, then fraud scoring.

The demand-based backpressure model is a hybrid of pull and push. It is pull because the subscriber pulls by calling `request(n)` to state how much it wants. It is push because once demand exists, the publisher pushes items via `onNext` without the subscriber asking for each one individually. The publisher must never send more `onNext` calls than the total requested, so if the subscriber requested ten and the publisher has sent ten, it must wait silently for another `request` call. A senior-level nuance is that the JDK ships `SubmissionPublisher<T>`, a ready-made `Publisher` backed by a bounded buffer and a `ForkJoinPool`; you rarely write a publisher from scratch, you use `SubmissionPublisher` and call its `submit(item)` method, and it handles the `request(n)` accounting and buffering for you. Another nuance is that the Flow API is purely a set of interfaces — the JDK deliberately did not ship operators like `map` or `filter`, because those belong to libraries like Reactor and RxJava that implement the same interfaces.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India there is a real-time transaction feed. During market hours thousands of card swipes, UPI payments and transfers stream in every second. A downstream fraud-verification desk must inspect each transaction, but verification is slow because it calls an external scoring model that takes time per transaction.

Problem 1 — the feed is far faster than the verifier. If the feed simply pushes every transaction to the verifier as fast as it arrives, the verifier's in-memory queue grows without bound until the service runs out of heap and crashes. This is exactly how a `Publisher` without backpressure behaves. The fix is for the `Subscriber` to call `Subscription.request(n)` so it only ever receives as many transactions as it has asked for. The verifier asks for a small batch, processes it, then asks for more.

Problem 2 — we also want to enrich each transaction with a calculated fee before it reaches the verifier, without coupling the feed to the fee logic. This is exactly what a `Processor` is for. We insert a `FeeEnrichmentProcessor` in the middle: it subscribes to the raw feed and republishes enriched transactions to the verifier. It passes the backpressure signal through, so if the verifier slows down, the processor slows down, and the raw feed slows down too.

Problem 3 — if the external scoring model throws an error, the whole stream must terminate cleanly and the verifier must be told. This is exactly what `onError` is for. And when the end-of-day feed closes, the verifier must know there is nothing more coming, which is exactly what `onComplete` is for.

The code will have a `Transaction` record for raw items, an `EnrichedTransaction` record after fee enrichment, a `FeeEnrichmentProcessor` that implements `Flow.Processor`, a `FraudVerifierSubscriber` that implements `Flow.Subscriber` and requests items in controlled batches, and a `FlowDemo` main class that uses the JDK `SubmissionPublisher` as the raw feed, wires the pipeline, submits several transactions for Rajesh and Priya, and shows the backpressure in action through log output.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is five transactions submitted to the raw feed: TXN-1 for Rajesh (SAV2001, 50000), TXN-2 for Priya (CUR3001, 25000), TXN-3 (SAV2001, 12000), TXN-4 (CUR3001, 80000) and TXN-5 (SAV2001, 3000). The verifier is slow and only wants two at a time.

Step 1 — `FlowDemo` creates a `SubmissionPublisher` as the raw feed, a `FeeEnrichmentProcessor`, and a `FraudVerifierSubscriber`, then wires feed to processor and processor to verifier. At this point the processor's `onSubscribe` runs and it calls `upstream.request(1)`, and the verifier's `onSubscribe` runs and it calls `subscription.request(2)`.

Step 2 — the demo calls `rawFeed.submit` for all five transactions. The `SubmissionPublisher` buffers them but only releases items into the processor as the processor's demand allows. The processor requested one, so TXN-1 flows in.

Step 3 — the processor's `onNext` receives TXN-1, computes fee as 0.1% of 50000 which is 50.00, builds an `EnrichedTransaction`, and calls `submit` to push it downstream. It then calls `upstream.request(1)` to pull TXN-2. The amount stays the same; only the fee is added.

Step 4 — the verifier's `onNext` receives the enriched TXN-1, sleeps 50 milliseconds to simulate the fraud-scoring call, logs the verification, and increments its batch counter to one. Because its batch size is two, it does not request more yet.

Step 5 — the enriched TXN-2 arrives at the verifier, it processes it, the batch counter reaches two, so it resets the counter and calls `subscription.request(2)` to pull the next batch. Only now do TXN-3 and TXN-4 flow through the processor and into the verifier. Backpressure held the later items back until the verifier was ready.

Step 6 — when all five are drained and the `SubmissionPublisher` closes (the try-with-resources block ends), the processor's `onComplete` fires and it calls `close()`, which triggers the verifier's `onComplete`. The stream ends cleanly.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Demo submits 5 txns: TXN-1..TXN-5 (Rajesh/Priya)
    │ rawFeed.submit(txn)  — backpressure-aware
    ▼
  SubmissionPublisher<Transaction>  (raw feed, bounded buffer)
    │ releases only as much as downstream demand allows
    ▼ onNext(Transaction)
  FeeEnrichmentProcessor  (Processor = Subscriber + Publisher)
    │ onSubscribe → upstream.request(1)
    │ fee = amount × 0.001   e.g. 50000 → 50.00
    │ submit(EnrichedTransaction) ; upstream.request(1)
    ▼ onNext(EnrichedTransaction)
  FraudVerifierSubscriber  (slow consumer, BATCH=2)
    │ onSubscribe → request(2)
    │ process (50ms fraud scoring) ×2
    │ after 2 done → request(2) more   ◄── BACKPRESSURE
    ▼
  onComplete() cascades: feed closes → processor.close() → verifier.onComplete()

  Demand signal travels UPSTREAM (request), items travel DOWNSTREAM (onNext)
  request(2) ◄─────────────── verifier
  request(1) ◄─── processor
  TXN flows ───────────────────────────► verifier (at most 2 in flight)
```

  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  [SUBMITTED] ──demand──→ [ENRICHED] ──demand──→ [VERIFIED]
       │                       │                      │
       │ upstream error        │ scoring error        │ done
       ▼                       ▼                      ▼
   [DROPPED]               [FAILED]             [onComplete]

  ── Call Chain ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. feed.subscribe(enricher)  → enricher.onSubscribe → request(1)
  2. enricher.subscribe(verifier) → verifier.onSubscribe → request(2)
  3. feed.submit(TXN-1) → enricher.onNext → submit(enriched) → upstream.request(1)
  4. verifier.onNext(enriched-1) → sleep 50ms → processed=1
  5. verifier.onNext(enriched-2) → processed=2 → request(2)
  6. feed close → enricher.onComplete → close() → verifier.onComplete

  Method Contract: Subscription.request(long n)
    Pre:  n > 0 (n <= 0 must signal onError per spec)
    Post: publisher may send up to n more onNext calls, never more
    Rule: total onNext sent <= total requested (strict backpressure)

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Flow API arrived in Java 9 as the JDK's standard adoption of the Reactive Streams specification. It is deliberately tiny — just four nested interfaces inside the `java.util.concurrent.Flow` class. A Publisher is a source that you subscribe to. A Subscriber is a consumer with four callbacks: on-subscribe, on-next for each item, on-error once if the stream fails, and on-complete once when it ends normally. A Subscription is the private channel between one publisher and one subscriber, and it carries the two most important methods of the whole model: request and cancel. A Processor is both a subscriber and a publisher, so you use it to build transformation stages in a pipeline.

The single idea that makes this different from a plain observer or a plain stream is demand-based backpressure. The consumer calls request with a number to say exactly how many items it is ready to receive, and the publisher is contractually forbidden from sending more on-next calls than the total the consumer has requested. So it is a hybrid of pull and push: the consumer pulls demand by calling request, and within that demand the publisher pushes items. This is what stops a fast producer from flooding a slow consumer and blowing up the heap.

In my banking work this solved a very real problem. We had a real-time transaction feed that produced far faster than our fraud-verification desk could consume, because verification calls a slow external scoring model. Without backpressure the verifier's queue grew until the service ran out of memory. I built a Flow pipeline where the JDK SubmissionPublisher was the raw feed, a fee-enrichment Processor sat in the middle to attach the fee, and a verifier Subscriber requested transactions only two at a time, asking for the next two only after finishing the current pair. The demand signal travelled upstream while the items travelled downstream, so the whole pipeline naturally ran at the speed of the slowest stage.

The nuance I always add is that the Flow API is only the contract — the JDK intentionally shipped no operators like map or filter, because those belong to libraries like Reactor and RxJava which implement the very same interfaces. In practice you rarely hand-write a Publisher; you use SubmissionPublisher, which already handles the demand accounting and buffering, and you focus on your Subscriber's request strategy. At National Bank of India, adopting this pattern turned an out-of-memory crash under load into a steady, self-regulating pipeline whose throughput was governed by the consumer, exactly as the Reactive Streams specification intends.
